newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durable goods orders surprisingly strong in February.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durable goods orders surprisingly strong in February.

text.p: Orders for costly manufactured goods posted a surprisingly strong gain last month, hitting record levels after a robust January, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday.

New orders for durable goods climbed 1.5 percent in February to a seasonally adjusted record $178.3 billion -- sharply contrary to Wall Street economists'expectations that orders would weaken by 0.4 percent.
The unexpected February orders pickup suggests the economy's industrial sector remains vigorous and may be gaining momentum.

The February increase followed a revised 4.1 percent increase in January orders, which previously was reported as a 4 percent rise. The surge in January orders was the strongest since a 4.5 percent rise last September.
Shipments of finished products also increased in February and order backlogs fattened for a ninth time in the past 10 months.

On Tuesday the Federal Reserve raised short-term interest rates by a quarter of percentage point, citing strong demand that the central bank said increased the risk of inflationary pressures. Its goal is to tamp down potential inflation by making credit slightly more costly without choking off growth.

"It sort of validates the Fed's feeling the economy is likely to overheat if they don't exercise a little restraint," said Robert McGee, senior economist at Tokai Bank Ltd. "The odds are they will do another (rate hike) in May unless something surprising happens to stop them."
"The chances of a May tightening are increasing every day with hawkish statements by the Fed and now these orders figures," added Fred Levin, chief economist at Eastbridge Capital Inc.

Durable goods are items like cars and home appliances that are intended to last at least three years. Since they take longer to manufacture and cost more to produce and buy, orders for them are a significant measure of manufacturing activity.
The biggest gain in February orders was for electronic and electrical equipment, up 7.4 percent to $30.6 billion after an even stronger 17.9 percent jump in January.
The department said that more demand for communications equipment and electronic components accounted for the order pickup in this category.
Industrial machinery and equipment orders rose for a third consecutive month, up 2.2 percent to $33.2 billion in February after a 0.9 percent January increase.

But transportation orders declined 3.6 percent to $40.8 billion after a 1.6 percent January rise. Commerce said there were declines in orders for all types of transportation items except railroad equipment in February.
Excluding transportation, durables orders rose last month by 3.1 percent to $137.5 billion after a 4.9 percent gain in January.
Orders for defence goods, which experience wide monthly swings, rose 0.1 percent to $6.3 billion following a 21.6 percent January plunge.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, an indication of business investment in new equipment, gained a strong 3.7 percent to $47.6 billion last month after a 4.5 percent surge in January.
Shipments of durable goods, an indication of current demand, climbed 1.4 percent to $173 billion after a 1.1 percent rise in January.
Unfilled orders increased 1.1 percent last month to $499.5 billion after a matching 1.1 percent January rise.
